behaviours.statement: A host with a trailing dot canonicalises to the same value as the host without it, so a denylist row matches both spellings.
Case is not part of a host; lower-casing is locale-independent, so the denylist does not miss on a Turkish-locale JVM.
Decimal, hexadecimal, long-octal, dotted-octal and short numeric spellings of loopback all canonicalise to 127.0.0.1.
A leading-zero part is octal as a browser reads it: 0177.0.0.1 is loopback and 012.0.0.1 is private, not the public addresses InetAddress.getByName would produce.
A host numeric in every part but out of range answers empty (a refusal the caller turns into 422), never the raw input passed through as a name.
A host containing an empty label cannot be canonicalised and fails closed rather than being tidied into something that resolves.
Normalisation never removes, merges or splits a label: notmalware.example.com and malware.example.com.evil.test survive intact and are never collapsed onto a denylisted parent.
Five numeric parts, or a part like 09 that is a number in no base read here, make a registered name rather than an address.
An IPv6 literal keeps its brackets and is only lower-cased, including the IPv4-mapped form that is refused today and must stay refused.
Normalisation is idempotent, so there is exactly one canonical form and no second form reachable by writing the first.
https://malware.example.com./x is refused with 422 url_rejected, byte-identical to the refusal for the same host without the trailing dot.
The denylisted host written in mixed case with a trailing dot is refused with the same 422: case and trailing dot are spellings, not separate evasions.
http://2130706433/ is refused with 422 url_rejected, byte-identical to the refusal for the dotted loopback form.
Every spelling in the harness's equivalent-form list — hex, octal, out-of-range numeric, trailing-dot names, IPv4-mapped IPv6 — is refused with 422 and one message.
A refused spelling mints nothing: no code is returned and the caller's link list is no longer than before.
Denylisted host, internal address, own origin and un-canonicalisable host all answer the same status, code and message, so the endpoint cannot read the denylist back.
Forms java.net.URI extracts no host from keep their 400 invalid_request; the 400/422 split does not move in either direction.
notmalware.example.com and malware.example.com.evil.test still yield links: tightening the check must not start refusing ordinary customer URLs.
A sub-domain of a denylisted host stays refused; normalising the host must not narrow denylist matching to an exact match.
An ordinary target is unaffected: the stored URL and the Location a click sends are byte-identical to what was submitted, because normalisation is for checking only.
A caller with no credentials posts an address and a password and gets 201 with the account id, the stored address and a creation instant.
The 201 carries no session token and no Location header, both deliberately absent.
The credentials just chosen work at the untouched session endpoint and return a token for the id sign-up returned.
That token is accepted by create, list, read, patch, delete and abuse-report — every endpoint an existing customer's token is accepted by.
Signing in with a case variant of the registered address returns the same account: an address is an identity, not a string.
The stored credential neither is nor contains the submitted password in any case, and is not a bare digest of it.
The stored form comes from the same password-holding mechanism at the same parameters as the seeded accounts, and that mechanism recognises the original password against it.
No response on the sign-up path — 201, 400 or 409 — echoes the password in any form.
A malformed address is refused with 400 invalid_request naming the field and the rule, and creates no account.
A password of exactly the minimum length is accepted and one character shorter is refused with 400 naming the rule, never the value.
A password of exactly the maximum length is accepted and can be signed in with; one character more is refused with 400.
A body missing or blanking either field is refused with 400 and creates nothing.
A property the operation does not define is refused with 400 rather than silently dropped.
A valid token, a forged token and no token produce the same result: the path is exempt from the session filter and has no 401.
GET, PUT, PATCH and DELETE on the accounts path answer 405 — not 401, and not a handler.
A second sign-up for an existing address is refused with 409 account_unavailable and storage still holds exactly one account under that name.
A case variant of an existing address is refused too: uniqueness is over the lower-cased address.
An address that arrived by migration is as taken as one created through the API, and the seeded account is untouched by the attempt.
When sign-ups for one address race, exactly one answers 201 and the rest 409 with no server error, and storage holds exactly one account afterwards.
After a refused duplicate, the original password still signs in and the loser's password does not: a duplicate never overwrites a stored credential.
The 409 body is the catalogue entry and nothing more: no holder, no date, no distinction between a two-year-old registration and a lost race.
Sign-ups from one address faster than the limit are refused with 429 rate_limited carrying Retry-After in whole seconds and never 0.
A throttled sign-up creates no account: the address it named is still free and no more accounts exist than the bucket allowed.
Duplicate attempts are metered by the same bucket, bounding the account enumeration the 409 necessarily permits.
Exhausting the sign-up bucket leaves sign-in served and vice versa: separate buckets under separate keys.
A newly created account's link list is empty and stays empty while other customers create links.
A self-signed-up customer naming another customer's code gets 404 not_found, byte-identical to an unissued code's answer and never 403.
A change of expiry on another customer's code answers 404 and the link's expiry is unchanged afterwards.
A delete on another customer's code answers 404 and the link keeps redirecting afterwards.
A self-signed-up customer's list and totals contain their own links and nobody else's, across every page.
The reverse direction: a seeded customer gets 404 for a self-signed-up customer's code and never sees it in a list.
A caller with no credentials posts a long URL and gets 201 with the code, the short URL in the same form the authenticated path returns, the unchanged target and both instants.
The response carries no status, no clickCount and no Location header, because none of them can ever be read back.
The stored link has no owner at all — not a placeholder account whose holder could list or delete it.
On default configuration the reported expiry is one month after creation, fixed at creation as an absolute instant.
An expiresAt property is refused with 400 rather than honoured or ignored: the expiry is the service's to set.
An alias property is refused with 400: codes are never reissued, so anonymous alias choice is permanent namespace squatting.
A missing, blank or non-absolute-http(s) target is refused with 400 invalid_request, as on the authenticated path.
A target longer than the configured ceiling is refused with 400, bounding the storage burn on an unauthenticated write path.
A denylisted target is refused with 422 url_rejected, byte-identical to the authenticated path's refusal for the same URL.
Internal, loopback, private and self-referential targets are refused with the same 422 and the same message.
Every equivalent-form spelling is refused here with 422 and every unparseable one keeps its 400: no second, laxer copy of the validation.
The same URL posted to both create paths gets the same verdict, across every refused and accepted target this suite knows.
A valid token, a forged token and no token all produce the same 201 and an equally unowned link; there is no 401 on this path.
Two anonymous creates for one target yield two different working codes, drawn from the same generator and not derived from the URL.
GET, PUT, PATCH and DELETE on the public links path answer 405 — not 401, and not a handler.
The reported expiry is the configured anonymous TTL after creation, whatever that TTL is set to.
The code redirects for the whole period it was promised and does not become unusable early.
After the expiry the code answers 404 not_found on the click path, and never 410.
That answer is byte-identical in status, body and cache headers to an unissued code's and to an expired owned link's.
A change of expiry naming the code answers 404 for every caller including its creator, and the link still stops working when it said it would.
A code that expires while its redirect is cached stops redirecting within the same bound the rest of the service is held to.
An anonymous code and an owned code with the same target produce the same status, Location and cache headers — 302 and never 301.
HEAD on an anonymous code answers with the same status and headers and no body, served by the same handler.
Presenting a credential when following an anonymous code changes nothing; the click path takes none either way.
After a known number of clicks and a flush, the durable count for an anonymous code equals the count for an owned code clicked as often.
Requests that 404 — after expiry, or for an unissued code — add nothing to an anonymous link's count.
Concurrent clicks on an anonymous link are all counted, with no loss under simultaneous traffic.
An anonymous code has the same length and alphabet as a generated owned code, so codes cannot be sorted into owned and unowned by shape.
Reading an anonymous code through the management API answers 404 for every signed-in caller, including one who just created it.
That 404 is byte-identical to an unissued code's and to another customer's code's: nobody's is not a distinguishable state.
Reading an anonymous code with no credential is refused as unauthenticated, exactly as any other code is, revealing nothing about the code.
A change of expiry answers 404 for every caller and the link is unchanged afterwards.
A delete answers 404 for every caller and the link keeps redirecting: this route is not a takedown for an unowned link.
The code appears on no page of any customer's list, seeded or newly created, and is counted in no customer's totals.
Creating anonymous links leaves an existing customer's list, totals and links exactly as they were — the regression surface for ownerless rows.
Creating anonymously past the limit is refused with 429 rate_limited carrying Retry-After in whole seconds and never 0.
A throttled anonymous create mints nothing: no code comes back and no more links exist than the bucket allowed.
With the anonymous bucket empty, a signed-in customer creating from the same address is unaffected: the buckets are separately keyed and namespaced.
A caller who has spent the authenticated write limit gains nothing by switching to the anonymous path: it meters them and refuses at its own capacity.
While the anonymous create bucket is empty, links already minted keep redirecting from the same address.
With the shared tier unreachable an anonymous create either succeeds or is refused with 503 service_unavailable, and never with any other server error.
The same target posted to both create paths during the outage gets the same verdict: the anonymous route neither survives an outage the authenticated one does not nor fails one it survives.
While anonymous creation is refused, clicks on anonymous links keep being served with the right target and cache headers.
Nothing on the click path answers 5xx during the outage for an anonymous code, live or unknown; 503 exists on the create paths only.
When the dependency returns, anonymous creation works again with no intervention and the link it mints redirects.
Reporting an anonymous code is accepted with 202 and the same body as reporting an owned one, saying nothing about existence or ownership.
A reported anonymous link stops redirecting within the published takedown bound, measured from the response.
Once blocked, the code answers the same 404 as an unissued one on the click path.
An unauthenticated report is still refused as unauthenticated — the residual gap that only an account holder can get an unowned link taken down, pinned rather than hidden.
Both seeded accounts sign in with their seeded credentials and get the tokens they got before.
Each seeded address exists exactly once after the change: the new lower-cased uniqueness constraint neither duplicated nor dropped a row.
A case variant of a seeded address still signs in and returns the same account, with no non-unique-result failure.
A seeded customer still creates, lists, reads, re-expires and deletes links exactly as documented before this change.
A seeded customer's stored credential is unchanged by other accounts being created, and the account still signs in afterwards.
An account created before the application restarts signs in after it with the same credentials and the same identity.
After a restart that customer lists the links they created and nothing else.
An anonymous link created before the restart still redirects to the same target afterwards — it cannot be recreated from a lost copy.
After the restart the management API still answers 404 for that code to every signed-in caller: ownership is not repaired by a boot.
An address taken before the restart is still refused with 409 afterwards: uniqueness lives in the database, not in a process.

harness.concern: How a test creates an account it can then sign in with and act as
harness.mechanism: AbstractIntegrationTest.givenAccount() / givenAccount(email, password) post to ApiClient.CUSTOMERS_PATH and return Fixtures.NewAccount(id, email, password), throwing loudly on any status but 201; sessionFor(NewAccount) delegates to ApiClient.sessionFor(email, password), which is the same request signInFor uses for a seeded customer. Addresses come from Fixtures.uniqueEmail(prefix) because the database outlives a class and a hard-coded address is taken on the second run.

harness.concern: How a test makes two sign-ups for one address genuinely race (AC6)
harness.mechanism: AbstractIntegrationTest.signUpConcurrently(email, password, attempts) builds one request per thread, holds them all on a CountDownLatch until every thread is ready, then releases them together and collects all responses. A loop would let each request complete before the next began, and a read-then-write implementation would pass it.

harness.concern: How a test creates an anonymous link it can then act on
harness.mechanism: AbstractIntegrationTest.givenAnonymousLink() / givenAnonymousLink(longUrl) post to ApiClient.PUBLIC_LINKS_PATH with no credential and return the parsed AnonymousLinkResponse (a distinct type from LinkResponse, so the absent status and clickCount show up as absent rather than null). ApiClient also offers createAnonymousLinkRaw for the alias/expiresAt refusals and createAnonymousLinkWithBearer for the no-401-by-construction case. createAnonymouslyRepeatedly(n) drives the rate-limit behaviours.

harness.concern: How a test observes an expired anonymous link without waiting a month, and without real time for owned links
harness.mechanism: An anonymous link's expiry is never caller-supplied, so AnonymousLinkExpiryTest overrides the service's own TTL with @SpringBootTest(properties = Fixtures.ANONYMOUS_TTL_KEY + "=PT3S") and calls givenExpiredAnonymousLink(), which waits past the instant the response reported and then clears the resolution cache. The new awaitExpiryOf(Instant) generalises the existing awaitExpiry(LinkResponse) so the two expiry types share one wait. No class may assume the override: without it givenExpiredAnonymousLink would sit for thirty days rather than fail.

harness.concern: How a test observes a click count that no endpoint will ever report (AC11)
harness.mechanism: AbstractIntegrationTest.storedClickCount(code) reads links.click_count over the injected DataSource, paired with awaitClickFlush() (two flush intervals plus a margin) or with the existing observeUntil. Raw SQL rather than a repository call because the repositories' owner-scoped queries are surface the implementing branch may reshape, whereas links.code and links.click_count are columns this change's migration does not touch. Behaviours compare an anonymous code against an owned code clicked the same number of times in the same test, so the claim is sameness rather than a remembered constant.

harness.concern: How a test observes that an anonymous link is owned by nobody, not by a hidden placeholder
harness.mechanism: AbstractIntegrationTest.storedLinkIsUnowned(code) reads (customer_id IS NULL) over the same DataSource. A service that homed anonymous links on a placeholder account would answer 404 to every HTTP request in this suite and still be wrong, because that account's list would contain them.

harness.concern: How a test observes what is stored for an account (AC6 'the stored data never contains two', AC7)
harness.mechanism: AbstractIntegrationTest.storedAccountsNamed(email) and storedPasswordHash(email) go through the frozen CustomerRepository, following the precedent PasswordStorageTest set with PasswordHasher: the repository is part of the contract both branches were built against, the schema is not. SignUpTest injects PasswordHasher to check the stored form recognises the original password and matches the seeded accounts' mechanism.

harness.concern: How a test restarts the application
harness.mechanism: Unchanged and not reinvented: NewSurfaceDurabilityTest extends AbstractRestartIntegrationTest, which boots the application itself with a SpringApplicationBuilder against the same JVM-wide containers and offers restartApplication(). That harness gained givenAnonymousLink(), givenAccount() and sessionFor(account) so the two new surfaces are reachable there without a second client; sessions are re-obtained after a restart because the signing key is ephemeral.

harness.concern: How a test asserts against the route at the root of the namespace
harness.mechanism: Unchanged: ApiClient.click(code), clickHead(code), clickWithBearer(code, bearer) and rootRequest(method, rawPath, body) are the only ways to reach /{code}, and no test builds that URL itself. Anonymous codes go through exactly these, which is what makes the AC11 comparison a comparison of one route rather than two.

harness.concern: How a test reaches a rate limit or a degraded dependency without waiting for production volumes
harness.mechanism: Unchanged mechanisms, new keys: Fixtures.SIGN_UP_LIMIT_KEY and Fixtures.ANONYMOUS_CREATE_LIMIT_KEY are driven down per class with @SpringBootTest(properties = ...), and resetSharedTierState() empties the JVM-wide buckets in @BeforeEach because both new buckets are keyed by client address and every test comes from loopback. Degradation uses TestInfrastructure.withCounterTierUnavailable, which pauses Redis and keeps the port mapping so recovery is observable.

harness.concern: How the 400-versus-422 split is kept from being invented twice
harness.mechanism: Fixtures.EQUIVALENT_FORM_URLS_REFUSED_AS_UNSHORTENABLE (host parses, so the host policy decides: 422) and Fixtures.URLS_REFUSED_AS_MALFORMED (java.net.URI yields no host, so the syntax gate decides: 400) are measured lists, not guesses — each entry was checked against java.net.URI on JDK 21 while writing this contract. Fixtures.LOOKALIKE_URLS_STILL_ACCEPTED carries the over-normalisation guard, and the LOOPBACK_HOST_SPELLINGS / UNCANONICALISABLE_HOSTS / NAMES_PRESERVED_BY_NORMALISATION lists quote HostNormalizer's worked table so the unit-level and HTTP-level behaviours cannot disagree about what canonical means.

rationale:
WHAT THIS IS. 15 test classes, 110 behaviours, zero assertions, all failing with fail("not implemented"); plus four harness files extended in place. `mvn -o clean test-compile` is BUILD SUCCESS on 41 test sources, and the one class that needs no containers was run to confirm the skeleton fails rather than passes (10 run, 10 failed, "not implemented"). Every acceptance criterion AC1-AC17 has at least one behaviour; AC17 is carried by the existing suite plus eleven regression behaviours that name the surfaces this change puts at risk (lookalike hosts still shortened, the 400/422 split unmoved, listings undisturbed by ownerless rows, seeded accounts, sign-in bucket, 405 on both exempted paths).

WHERE I EXTENDED THE HARNESS RATHER THAN LET THE NEXT NODE INVENT IT. Four mechanisms were genuinely new and all four are the kind that fail only after both branches have merged: creating an account and signing in as it; racing sign-ups from a released latch; reaching an anonymous link's expiry, which is not caller-supplied and therefore requires the service's own TTL to be configured down; and observing a click count for a link no endpoint will ever report. The last one is the only place I put SQL in this suite, and I want a reviewer to weigh it rather than skim it. AC11 says an anonymous link's clicks are counted by the same mechanism, and AC13 says nobody may ever read that number — the two together mean the claim is unobservable through the API by construction. The choices were to read links.click_count directly, to read it through a repository the implementing branch may reshape, or to drop AC11's counting half to a structural argument ("it is the same handler") that no test proves. I took the column, on the reasoning that links.code and links.click_count are not touched by this change's migration, and confined the DataSource to two helpers with the justification in their javadoc. If a reviewer would rather the suite never touched the schema, the honest alternative is to accept that AC11's counting half is argued and not demonstrated; say so now, because it is a harness decision and after this node it is a re-freeze.

WHAT I DID NOT COVER, AND WHY. (1) AC3's "fails against the pre-change code" is not, and cannot be, a method: no test can state something about its own history. HostEvasionRefusalTest and HostCanonicalisationTest are the tests AC3 names, they are expected to fail against the code as it stands, and the before-and-after evidence has to come from the run record — which means someone must actually run them before `implement` lands, or AC3 is unmet with a green suite. That is a pipeline obligation, not a coding one, and it is the single easiest thing here to lose. (2) The design's no-retroactive-rescan decision (A4) — links already minted through the newly refused forms keep redirecting — is untestable through this harness, because there is no longer any way to mint one: the only route would be inserting a row behind the API, which would be the suite writing the data it then reads. It is stated in the design's rationale and on the operation, and it stays a documented consequence rather than a behaviour. (3) The limiter fails open when Redis is unreachable, so during an outage both new unauthenticated endpoints are unmetered, including a memory-hard hash per sign-up. AnonymousCreateDegradationTest pins that the click path never degrades, but no behaviour asserts what the buckets do while their store is down — pinning fail-open in a test would make a deliberate, reviewable availability choice expensive to revisit, and it is not what any AC asks for. (4) The IP-keyed buckets cannot be shown to be per-caller: every test in this suite comes from loopback, so "one address is throttled while another is served" is only demonstrated for the customer-keyed write bucket, which the existing suite already does. Behind a proxy that does not preserve the source address these become global ceilings; that belongs in the runbook and is out of reach here. (5) The concurrency behaviour (B39) proves exactly one account exists after a race, but it cannot force a particular interleaving — it will pass against a correct constraint and fail against a read-then-write only probabilistically. Running it repeatedly is worth more than any single run, and the storage check is what makes even one run meaningful.

TWO THINGS THE NEXT TWO NODES SHOULD READ AS BINDING. First, the 400-versus-422 split. I measured every evasion fixture against java.net.URI on JDK 21 rather than reasoning about it, and it does not line up with HostNormalizer's javadoc table in the way one would guess: 999.999.999.999, 1.2.3.4.5, 127.1, 0x7f.0.0.1 and a..b yield a null host and therefore stay 400 at the HTTP level, while 4294967296 parses as a host and therefore reaches the host policy and is 422. The normaliser's table and the HTTP table are both correct and they are about different stages; anyone who conflates them will write a behaviour that cannot pass. That is why the two are separate named lists in Fixtures and why the unit-level class exists at all. Second, "account name" is the email address throughout — every sign-up behaviour is written on that reading. If the architect rules for a separate username, this contract does not survive an edit; it needs re-freezing, and the cost of finding out after the branches split is both of them.
